Vinyl-Addition Polymerizations of Borylated Allenes
Brian P. Jacobs and Johnathan N. Brantley *
Cite This: Macromolecules 2021, 54, 8822 −8828 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: Borylated motifs hold immense potential for
functional soft materials, as they can facilitate a range of reaction
manifolds (e.g., analyte binding or cross-coupling). Traditional
boron-containing materials are predominantly composed of either
aryl boronates or main-chain embedded vinylic boronates. Progress
toward expanding the architectural (and, by extension, functional)
scope of borylated polymers remains slightly limited. To address
this, we report the vinyl-addition polymerization of an allenylbor-
onic acid pinacol ester. The base metal catalyst, [( η3-C
3H5)Ni-
(OC(O)CF3)]2, was found to readily polymerize this allene
monomer with good regioselectivity and molecular weight control.
Additionally, the allenylboronate monomer could be copolymerized with other allenes (e.g., 1,2-nonadiene or β-pinadiene) to access
an array of borylated materials. The borylated polyallenes could also be chemically tailored under mild conditions (e.g., using Pd-
catalyzed cross-coupling), which suggests that they could serve as general platforms for accessing diverse architectures.
■ INTRODUCTION
Soft materials that incorporate main group elements often
exhibit unique physical or chemical properties, and synthetic
access to these sca ﬀolds has long been a focus in polymer
science. Borylated polymers are particularly attractive targets,
as boronates can exhibit a broad range of reactivity
manifolds.1−14 This fact is well established for small molecule
chemistry, where boron-containing substrates are key compo-
nents of C −C bond-forming reactions (e.g., Suzuki −
Miyaura,4−6 Matteson,8−10 Brown,11,12 or Zweifel13 chemistry)
that have profoundly transformed the art of organic synthesis.
Additionally, the Lewis acidity of boron is routinely exploited
for the development of chemosensors.
14 Interfacing borylated
motifs with polymers is increasingly a key design element in
the development of advanced materials, 15−21 and recent
progress has showcased boron-containing polymers in a variety
of applications. 22−38
While these precedents demonstrate the versatility of
unifying boron chemistry with polymer science, there are
lingering obstacles to the preparation of borylated materials.
For example, the synthetic scope is largely limited to polymers
derived from aromatic boronates (although materials bearing
aliphatic boronates were recently prepared using radical
24,25 or
metal-catalyzed polymerizations 26).15−21 Jäkle reported early
examples of preparing well-de ﬁned borylated polystyrenes
either through a substituent exchange reaction 15 or through
ATRP.16 Summerlin would later elaborate this work by
developing RAFT polymerizations of styrene monomers that
were functionalized with boronic esters ( Figure 1 A).17
Polyacrylamides18 and polylactides 35 decorated with aryl
boronate derivatives have also been prepared through radical
polymerization or Miyaura-borylation, respectively ( Figure
1B). Controlled access to polymers exhibiting vinylic sp 2 C−
B bonds, however, is slightly more limited in scope. Initial
eﬀorts by Chujo detailed the hydroboration polymerization of
bifunctional boranes across a π-conjugated enediyne synthon
to furnish fully conjugated organoborane polymers. 19 Qin
elaborated further on this methodology by employing trans-
enediynes as coupling partners, yielding borylated polyacety-
lenes ( Figure 1 C).33 Notably, these strategies a ﬀorded vinylic
boronates within the polymer sca ﬀold (which enabled tuning
of optoelectronic properties). 21 However, current methods for
incorporating vinyl boronates into polymers impose certain
restrictions. For example, such materials are limited to
alternating copolymers, and reported examples feature low
molecular weights (<13,000 Da). Given our recent interest in
exploring the interface of small molecule chemistry and
borylated polymers,
28 we reasoned that these platforms are
not well suited for chemical tailoring (as cross-coupling
through the boronate in the main chain could destroy the
polymer). Thus, we envisioned that new approaches for
generating polymers that are decorated with chemically
addressable vinyl boronates would represent a signi ﬁcant
advancement.

We surmised that vinyl-addition polymerization of borylated
allenes could represent an unexplored route to address this
challenge. Endo has reported that [( η
3-C3H5)Ni(OC(O)-
CF3)]2 catalyzes the living vinyl-addition polymerizations of
allenes decorated with an array of functional groups, 39−41 and
sterically encumbered monomers often exhibit excellent
regioselectivity for 2,3-insertions. Given this precedent, we
hypothesized that bulky allenyl boronates (e.g., pinacol esters)
would exhibit similar regioselectivity during vinyl-addition
polymerizations to aﬀord C(sp
2)vinyl−B motifs in the side chain
of the repeating unit ( Figure 1 ). Realization of this process
would allow for the generation of polymers bearing vinylic
boronates that could permit both (i) tailored copolymer
generation and (ii) post-polymerization modi ﬁcations of the
pendant vinyl boronates for further structural diversi ﬁcation.
■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Polymerization Optimization. Allenylboronic acid pina-
col ester 1 was selected for our preliminary investigations,
given that (i) the pinacol ester should be su ﬃciently
encumbering to promote the desired 2,3-regioselectivity and
(ii) 1 can be readily synthesized on multigram scales.
42 Our
polymerization studies commenced by evaluating the e ﬃcacy
of common vinyl-addition polymerization catalysts ( Table 1 ,
entries 1 −3). We initially focused on [( η3-C3H5)Ni(OC(O)-
CF3)]2 (3; prepared in situ; see Supporting Information), given
that it has been shown to polymerize allenes with excellent
regioselectivity and functional group compatibility.
39−41 1H
NMR spectroscopy (toluene- d8) revealed 99% consumption of
1 ([1]o = 0.5 M) in the presence of 3 after 1.5 h at 23 °C. The
mixture was then ﬁltered through basic alumina and
concentrated to dryness to a ﬀord polymer 2 as a colorless
solid (92% yield). Analysis by gel permeation chromatography
(GPC) revealed that 2 exhibited a number average molecular
weight ( Mn) that was in good agreement with the targeted
value (cf. 27,260 vs 30,000 Da, respectively). 1H NMR
spectroscopic analysis of 2 was consistent with the expected
product regioselectivity to a ﬀord vinyl boronates in the
repeating unit, as we observed a broad vinyl resonance ( δ
5.26 ppm) that integrated to 1 H (relative to the pinacol
methyl groups). The expected allylic methylene proton
resonances ( δ 2.5−3.5 ppm) and pinacol methyl proton
resonances ( δ 1.16 ppm) were also observed ( Figure 2 ).
Furthermore, DEPTQ NMR spectroscopic analysis of 2 was

consistent with the proposed repeating unit ( Figure S17 ).
Speciﬁcally, one vinyl resonance ( δ 116.1 ppm) was associated
with a C(sp 2)−H group, while the other vinyl resonance ( δ
161.7 ppm) was associated with a quaternary center. If the
polymerization proceeded by 1,2-insertion, we would expect
that one vinyl resonance would be associated with a C(sp
2)−
H2 center. As such, our combined NMR studies were
consistent with the expected 2,3-polymerization of 1.
Closer inspection of the broad resonances in the 1H NMR
spectrum revealed major and minor resonances within each
range. Integration of these ranges revealed a consistent ratio of
1 vinyl proton to 2 methylene protons in each set of
resonances ( Figures S19 and S20 ); thus, we did not attribute
these minor resonances to products of 1,2-insertions. Instead,
we hypothesized that these minor resonances ( δ 2.49−2.72
and 5.04−5.13 ppm) could have originated from ( Z)-insertion
of the allene during the polymerization. Importantly, the
corresponding
11B NMR spectrum displayed a broad
resonance ( δ 24.25 ppm; Figure S21 ), which indicated
retention of the boronate ester within the isolated polymer. 43
Further solid-state analyses of the isolated polymer were
conducted to assess some of the bulk material properties of
product 2. Thermogravimetric analysis of homopolymer 2
revealed a decomposition onset temperature of 255 °C( Figure
S8), and dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) of a powder
sample revealed T
g = 147 °C (determined using tan( δ)max;
Figure S9). This value was further corroborated by di ﬀerential
scanning calorimetry, which revealed a transition at 148 °C
(Figure S10 ).
Having demonstrated successful polymerization of 1,w e
sought to brie ﬂy survey the e ﬃcacy of other vinyl-addition
polymerization catalysts. We focused on trans-(C6F5)2Ni-
(SbPh3)2 (5) and a cationic Ni-allyl catalyst that is highly
active in the vinyl-addition polymerizations of ole ﬁns ( 4;
generated by activating 3 with AgSbF 6).44 Catalyst 4 aﬀorded
the desired product in an acceptable yield (52%; Table 1, entry
2), but GPC analysis revealed a bimodal product distribution
(Figure S2 ). Catalyst 5 displayed low reactivity toward the
polymerization of 1, with only 8% yield of the polymer isolated
after 1.5 h ( Table 1 , entry 3). Moreover, addition of this
reaction mixture to MeOH precipitated a solid that was
sparingly soluble in common organic solvents (which
precluded further analyses).
Given these outcomes, we elected to use 3 for our
subsequent optimization studies. We initially surveyed various
solvents to identify their impact on the target polymerization
(Table 1 , entries 4 −8). Tetrahydrofuran (THF) a ﬀorded
polymer 2 in yield similar to toluene ( Table 1 , entry 4), but
GPC analysis of the THF-derived product revealed a bimodal
distribution of products ( Figure S3 ). Diethyl ether provided
the product in high isolated yield ( Table 1 , entry 5), but the
observed M
n greatly exceeded the target (cf. 35,180 vs 30,000
Da, respectively). Dichloromethane (DCM), however, af-
forded a low dispersity material in high yield ( Table 1 , entry
7), and the observed M
n was in excellent agreement with the
target value (cf. 29,450 vs 30,000 Da). As such, DCM was
selected as our solvent of choice for subsequent studies. 45
With our selected polymerization conditions in hand, we
successfully prepared materials exhibiting a range of molecular
weights (M
n = 24,070−130,800 Da; D̵= 1.42−1.70) in modest
to good yields (69 −87%; Table S1 ). We note that dilute
conditions ([ 1]o = 0.1 M) were necessary to access higher Mn
materials with good control over molecular weight and
dispersity. For example, when targeting a material with Mn =
100,000 Da under our standard concentration ([ 1]o = 0.5 M),
we obtained a polymer with a measured Mn that far exceeded
the target (Mn = 130,800 Da; Figure S5). Conducting the same
polymerization using [ 1]o = 0.1 M, however, a ﬀorded a
material with a measured Mn that more closely matched the
theoretical value ( Mn = 90,350 Da; Figure S6 ).
Living Character Studies. Having demonstrated success-
ful vinyl-addition polymerizations of 1, we sought to determine
if the reaction exhibited living character. We monitored Mn as a
function of monomer conversion, which revealed a linear

correlation consistent with a living polymerization ( Figure 3A).
Additionally, the dispersity values narrowed considerably with
increasing monomer conversion, further implicating the living
nature of this polymerization. 46 To further explore the nature
of the polymerization, we also conducted a chain extension
experiment ( Figure 3 B; see Supporting Information ). Brie ﬂy,
the polymerization of 1 was monitored by
1HN M R
spectroscopy, until complete consumption of the monomer
was observed, after which an aliquot was removed and
analyzed by GPC. A second portion of 1 was added to the
polymerization, and the reaction was again monitored by
1H
NMR spectroscopy. Upon consumption of the added
monomer, an aliquot was removed for GPC analysis. This
sequence was repeated an additional time, and the GPC data
were consistent with successful chain extensions ( Table S3 ).
Lastly, a low M
n sample of 2 was prepared ( Mn = 4865 Da,
1.45 D̵; Figure S7 ) for end-group analysis via 1H NMR
spectroscopy ( Figure S18 ).48 Using the allyl resonances as
diagnostic handles, the calculated Mn (Mn = 3363 Da) was in
good agreement with the value obtained from GPC (which
suggested high end-group ﬁdelity).These experiments suggest
that the polymerization has a living character, but the dispersity
(D̵> 1.47) of the resultant polymers indicates that molecular
weight control could be slightly limited ( Tables 1 and S2).
47
Block Copolymerizations with Additional Allenes.
Because the polymerization of allene 1 was shown to exhibit a
living character, e ﬀorts turned toward the generation of block
copolymers. Copolymerizations of 1 with alkyl allenes struck
us as an enticing target, 39−41,49,50 as the resultant materials
could be considered borylated congeners of polyole ﬁns. We
selected 1,2-nonadiene as the comonomer for a preliminary
study, given that this allene has recently been reported to
undergo vinyl-addition polymerization under the action of 3
(Figure 4 ).
49 A block copolymerization was conducted under
conditions that targeted an ultimate Mn = 100,000 Da (50,000
Da per block; Figure 4A; see Supporting Information). Brieﬂy,
1 was ﬁrst polymerized under the action of 3. Upon complete
consumption of the monomer (as determined by NMR
spectroscopy), 1,2-nonadiene was added to the polymerization
mixture. The ﬁnal block copolymer, 6, was precipitated from
MeOH after 2 h (46% yield; Table 2 ). Importantly,
1H NMR
spectroscopic analysis con ﬁrmed the successful incorporation
of 1 into 6 (31 vs 43% predicted; vide inf ra). GPC analysis of 6
revealed that Mn was in modest agreement with the expected
value ( Figure 4 B; Mn = 80,510 vs 100,000 Da predicted; D̵=
1.43), and thermogravimetric analysis of the freshly precipi-
tated material revealed that 6 exhibited good thermal stability
(cf. T
d = 331 °C for 6 vs 255 °C for 2; Figure S14 ).
Unfortunately, the waxy nature of 6 precluded further

evaluation of thermomechanical properties using DMA. Given
that poly(1,2-nonadiene) has a degradation onset at
approximately 325 °C,
49 incorporation of this motif into 6
could be the origin of the enhanced thermal stability relative to
homopolymer 2.
We also prepared a block copolymer of 1 and a biomass-
derived monomer to access a material that could be considered
a novel analogue of cyclic ole ﬁn copolymers. We selected the
terpene-derived allene, β-pinadiene, for our e ﬀorts (as this
monomer has recently been shown to undergo living vinyl-
addition polymerizations with 3
50). Copolymerization of 1 and
β-pinadiene was conducted in a manner similar to the
procedure described above, and we ultimately isolated block
copolymer 7 as a faint-yellow powder (71% yield; Figure 4C).
Moderate incorporation of monomer 1 was determined by
1H
NMR spectroscopic analysis (37 vs 49% predicted). GPC
analysis of 7 revealed a lower M
n than expected (cf. 66,460 vs
100,000 Da, respectively) and a slightly broader dispersity
relative to block copolymer 6 (Table 2 ). The thermal stability
of freshly precipitated 7 increased relative to homopolymer 2
(cf. Td = 273 vs 255 °C; Figure S15 ), and DMA of a powder
sample revealed a higher Tg value as well (cf. 161 vs 147 °C;
Figure S16 ). As in the case of product 6, the physical
properties of 7 seemed to be dominated by the comonomer.
We were intrigued by the fact that incorporation of 1 into
both block copolymers was lower than expected, even though
1 was fully consumed during both reactions. This fact,
combined with modest isolated yields for both 6 and 7,
suggested to us that incomplete chain extension could explain
our observations. To probe this, we conducted a synthesis of 6
as described above, precipitated the solid polymer from
MeOH, and collected the supernatant. Concentration of this
supernatant to dryness a ﬀorded a colorless powder, and
1H
NMR spectral analysis revealed that this solid was homopol-
ymer 2 (which is highly soluble in MeOH). Similarly, 2 was
isolated from the supernatant following precipitation of freshly
prepared 7. In both cases, the recovered mass of all polymeric
products exceeded 74%. Interestingly, switching the order of
monomer addition (i.e., 1,2-nonadiene or β-pinadiene was
polymerized before adding 1 to the reaction) also resulted in
the formation of 2 with a minimal impact on the total
recovered mass of polymeric products (see Table S4 , Figures
S30 and S31). These data, along with the increase in D ̵that we
observed upon chain extension ( Figure 4 ), suggest that chain
transfer of the active polym erization catalyst could be
operative. The mechanism (and catalyst speciation) that
gives rise to this putative activity is currently being
investigated.
Post-polymerization Modi ﬁcation. Given that 2 is
decorated with vinyl boronates, we also explored methods
for chemically modifying the polymer to demonstrate the
synthetic versatility of these motifs. We chose to investigate
Suzuki−Miyaura cross-coupling, given the preponderance of
recent literature regarding the interfacing of this synthetic
method with material science.
28,35,51,52 Polymer 2 exhibits
some homology to polyole ﬁns, and we envisaged that
successfully merging cross-coupling with our new polymer
platform may enable rapid access to diversi ﬁed, functional
polyoleﬁn products. As a simple demonstration of this
approach, the cross-coupling of 2 with phenyl bromide was
evaluated (Figure 5). The coupled product, 8, was obtained as
a solid in high conversion (96%) and excellent yield (93%),
and
1H NMR spectroscopic analysis was consistent with the
expected product ( Figure S32).39 Gratifyingly, GPC analysis of
8 indicated that the cross-coupling proceeded with high ﬁdelity
and minimal changes to overall material dispersity (cf. D̵=
1.86 vs 1.87 for 8 and 2, respectively; Figure 5). The success of
this protocol suggests that non-aryl sp 2 C−B motifs could
become useful linchpins that engender polymeric sca ﬀolds with
intrinsic tunability.
■ CONCLUSIONS
Borylated polymers that bear arene and vinylic sp 2 C−B motifs
have demonstrated considerable versatility, underscoring the
importance of pursuing new routes to access these sca ﬀolds.
We have detailed the vinyl-addition polymerization of the
borylated allene monomer 1 to generate a polymer that is
decorated with vinyl boronates. The polymerization exhibited
living characteristics, and block copolymers of 1 and other
allenes (i.e., 1,2-nonadiene and β-pinadiene) were successfully
prepared. Lastly, we have shown that simple Suzuki −Miyaura
cross-coupling is possible with polymer 2 to a ﬀord functional
polyoleﬁn surrogates in a facile manner. We envision that our
